states.umLimits: At least the Section 32-7-6(c) bodily-injury limits (25/50). Underinsured vehicles are within the statutory definition of 'uninsured motor vehicle', so underinsured motorist coverage travels with uninsured motorist coverage.
states.effective: 25/50/25 in current Ala. Code 32-7-6(c); no 2024-2026 change found on the Legislature's code site.
states.note: Alabama requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Uninsured/underinsured-motorist coverage is included unless you turn it down.
states.uncertain: Ala. Code 32-7-23(a) says only that the named insured 'shall have the right to reject' uninsured motorist coverage; it does not itself say the initial rejection must be in writing (writing is mentioned only for re-requesting coverage on renewal). Underinsured motorist coverage inclusion is via the 32-7-23(b)(4) definition (text seen truncated: 'The sum of the limits of liability under all bodily inj...'). Medical payments coverage/PIP 'not required' is based on absence of any mandate found, not an express statute.

states.umLimits: Combined uninsured/underinsured coverage in the AS 28.22.101(d) amounts (50/100 bodily injury, 25 property damage); may be waived in writing in whole or in part (AS 21.96.020(e)).
states.effective: 50/100/25 in current AS 28.22.101(d) and AS 28.20.440(b)(2); no 2024-2026 change found.
states.note: Alaska requires at least $50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Uninsured/underinsured-motorist coverage at those same amounts is included unless you waive it in writing.
states.uncertain: AS 28.22.011(a)(1)-(2) exempts some vehicles driven only in areas not connected to the main road system (for drivers without recent serious violations); “insurance required” describes the general case. Medical payments coverage/PIP 'not required' is based on absence of any mandate found.

states.umLimits: Insurer must offer uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage by written notice on a director-approved form, up to the policy's bodily-injury limits; purchase is optional (A.R.S. 20-259.01, titled 'uninsured optional; underinsured optional').
states.effective: 25/50/15 for policies issued or renewed beginning July 1, 2020 (was 15/30/10). No later change found.
states.note: Arizona requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $15,000 for property damage. Your insurer has to offer uninsured and underinsured-motorist coverage in writing, but buying it is your choice.
states.uncertain: Medical payments coverage/PIP 'not required' is based on absence of any mandate found (20-259.01(J) mentions medical payments coverage only in the context of liens).

states.pipAmount: Medical and hospital benefits up to $5,000 per person, income-disability benefits, and a $5,000 accidental-death benefit (A.C.A. 23-89-202); any or all parts may be rejected in writing (23-89-203).
states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist bodily-injury coverage not less than the 27-19-605 limits; insurer must offer higher limits up to the insured's liability limits. Underinsured motorist coverage must be offered (may be rejected in writing) and can only be issued together with uninsured motorist coverage.
states.effective: 25/50/25 in current A.C.A. 27-22-104 (Lexis public-access Arkansas Code, viewed 2026-09-22). No 2024-2026 change found.

sources.label: Arkansas Insurance Department, Consumers FAQ: "What coverages are mandatory?"
A.C.A. 27-22-104 (Lexis public access, search for the section)
A.C.A. 23-89-403 (Lexis public access, search for the section)
A.C.A. 23-89-209 (Lexis public access, search for the section)
A.C.A. 23-89-202 and 23-89-203 (Lexis public access, search for the section)

states.note: Arkansas requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Personal injury protection and uninsured-motorist coverage come with your policy unless you turn them down in writing, and underinsured-motorist coverage must be offered to you.
states.uncertain: The limits are confirmed on the Arkansas Insurance Department's Consumers FAQ ("What coverages are mandatory?"). The official Arkansas Code is only published through LexisNexis public access, which blocks direct links behind a captcha, so the statute quotes come from Lexis search-result excerpts and the full sections weren't seen. The uninsured motorist coverage quote joins two excerpts; the word 'not' is bracketed because the connecting text was cut off. Exact PIP income-disability figures were not captured. Medical payments coverage 'not required' means no separate mandate was found (PIP covers medical).

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage required in every bodily-injury liability policy unless deleted by written agreement in a statutory form, or reduced by agreement but not below the Veh. Code 16056 minimums. Underinsured motorist coverage must be included in all policies that provide uninsured motorist coverage (Ins. Code 11580.2(p)(7)).
states.effective: 30/60/15 for policies issued or renewed on or after Jan 1, 2025 (was 15/30/5). Scheduled: for policies issued or renewed on or after Jan 1, 2035, minimums rise by $20,000/$40,000/$10,000 (to 50/100/25).

scheduledChanges.summary: Vehicle Code 16056(d) raises each minimum by $20,000/$40,000/$10,000, to $50,000/$100,000/$25,000, for policies issued or renewed from 1 January 2035.

states.note: California requires at least $30,000 per person and $60,000 per accident for injuries, plus $15,000 for property damage, for policies issued or renewed since January 1, 2025. Uninsured and underinsured-motorist coverage is included unless you sign a form removing it. The minimums are set to rise again in 2035.
states.uncertain: Financial responsibility can also be met by a bond, cash deposit, or self-insurance (Veh. Code 16021), not only insurance. Medical payments coverage 'not required' is based on absence of any mandate found.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage at least the 42-7-103(2) bodily-injury limits; uninsured motorist coverage by statute includes underinsured-motorist coverage (10-4-609(4)). Insurer must offer uninsured motorist coverage equal to the insured's bodily-injury limits. Medical payments coverage: $5,000 unless rejected in writing (or in the same medium as the application).
states.effective: 25/50/15 in C.R.S. 10-4-620 (section added 2003, effective July 1). No change found through the 2024 statutes.
states.note: Colorado requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $15,000 for property damage. Uninsured/underinsured-motorist coverage and $5,000 of medical payments coverage are included unless you turn them down in writing.
states.uncertain: The source is the Legislature's 2024 CRS Title 10 PDF (an 'Uncertified Printout'); a 2025 edition was not found at the same path, so 2025-2026 session changes were not checked against statute text. The medical payments coverage rejection may also be made 'in the same medium' as the application, not strictly on paper.

states.umLimits: Combined uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage required in every policy. It defaults to your bodily-injury liability limits. You may request a lower amount in writing with a signed informed-consent form, but never below the 14-112(a) minimums (25/50). Insurers must offer twice the bodily-injury limits.
states.effective: 25/50/25 in current Conn. Gen. Stat. 14-112(a), incorporated by 38a-335(a). No 2024-2026 change found.
states.note: Connecticut requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Every policy must include uninsured/underinsured-motorist coverage. It matches your liability limits unless you sign a form lowering it, and it can't go below $25,000/$50,000.
states.uncertain: Connecticut repealed its no-fault/PIP system, so PIP is not required. Medical payments coverage 'not required' is based on absence of any mandate found.

states.pipAmount: At least $15,000 per person and $30,000 per accident (medical, lost earnings, funeral up to $5,000, etc.), 21 Del. C. 2118(a)(2). Also required: $10,000 minimum PIP-style coverage for damage to property other than vehicles (2118(a)(3)).
states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage at least the financial-responsibility minimums for bodily injury and property damage (property damage subject to a $250 deductible). Insurer must offer additional coverage up to 100/300; underinsured motorist coverage is part of that optional additional coverage.
states.effective: 25/50/10 in 21 Del. C. 2902(b)(2), incorporated by 2118(a)(1). No 2024-2026 change found.
states.note: Delaware requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $10,000 for property damage. You must also carry personal injury protection (at least $15,000 per person and $30,000 per accident). Uninsured-motorist coverage is included unless you turn it down in writing, and underinsured coverage is an option you can buy.
states.uncertain: Delaware PIP pays regardless of fault, but no tort threshold was found in the text reviewed, so it isn't marked as a no-fault state (PIP is an add-on here). Medical payments coverage 'not required' is based on absence of a separate mandate (PIP covers medical).

states.pipAmount: Optional. Insurers must offer PIP (medical/rehabilitation, work loss, funeral), and the insured may buy any or all parts (D.C. Code 31-2404).
states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage required at $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident bodily injury and $5,000 property damage ($200 deductible). Optional higher uninsured motorist coverage up to 100/300/25. Underinsured motorist coverage is optional; insurers must offer it and need not keep written rejections.
states.effective: Current: 25/50/10. Scheduled: D.C. Law 26-155 (Motor Vehicle Insurance Modernization Amendment Act of 2026) applies as of Oct 1, 2027. It raises liability to $50,000/$100,000 and property damage to $20,000, raises uninsured motorist coverage to 50/100/20, requires underinsured motorist coverage or enhanced underinsured motorist coverage (with waiver options), and adds increases every 10 years starting Jan 1, 2037.

scheduledChanges.summary: D.C. Law 26-155 raises the minimums to $50,000/$100,000/$20,000 (and uninsured-motorist coverage to match) for policies from 1 October 2027.

states.note: D.C. requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $10,000 for property damage. Uninsured-motorist coverage is mandatory, while personal injury protection and underinsured coverage are options. A new law raises the minimums to $50,000/$100,000/$20,000 starting October 1, 2027.
states.uncertain: D.C. Is a "choice" no-fault system: PIP is optional, and the lawsuit limit in 31-2405(b) applies only if an injured person with PIP elects PIP benefits. Without PIP you're under ordinary fault rules, so the default is not no-fault. No uninsured motorist coverage rejection provision was found in 31-2406, so uninsured motorist coverage is marked required. Medical payments coverage 'not required' is based on absence of any mandate found.

states.pipAmount: $10,000 in medical and disability benefits (pays 80% of reasonable medical expenses) plus $5,000 death benefit
states.umLimits: Applies only to policies that include bodily injury liability. Uninsured motorist coverage limits must equal your bodily injury limits unless you pick lower limits or reject uninsured motorist coverage in writing. Florida's uninsured motorist coverage also covers underinsured drivers: s. 627.727(3)(b) treats an at-fault driver with too little bodily injury coverage as 'uninsured'. The minimum PIP + property damage policy has no bodily injury, so uninsured motorist coverage is not part of it.
states.effective: Property damage $10,000 (s. 324.022) and PIP $10,000 (s. 627.736) are current. Repeal bills in the 2026 session (SB 522 / HB 769) would have ended no-fault and required 25/50 bodily injury. SB 522 'Died in Banking and Insurance'. No change enacted.

sources.label: Fla. Stat. s. 324.021(7) (BI proof only after crash / FR events)

states.note: Florida doesn't make most drivers carry bodily-injury liability. You need $10,000 of personal injury protection (PIP), which pays your own medical bills no matter who caused the crash, plus $10,000 of property damage liability. If you add bodily-injury coverage, uninsured-motorist coverage comes with it unless you turn it down in writing.
states.uncertain: Bodily-injury limits are blank because Florida doesn't require them when you register a car. They become required ($10,000/$20,000 under s. 324.021(7)) only after certain crashes or violations, and DUI convictions trigger higher amounts under s. 324.023 (not re-read here). Uninsured motorist coverage is marked not required because the table describes a minimum policy: s. 627.727 attaches uninsured-motorist coverage (unless rejected in writing) only to policies that include bodily-injury liability, and a PIP-plus-property-damage policy doesn't.

states.effective: 25/50/25 has not changed. SB 121 (2025, signed) created O.C.G.A. 33-7-16, which requires 50/100/50 after a first DUI conviction and 100/300/100 after a second, for convictions on or after the Act's approval. It does not change the general minimum.

sources.label: Georgia Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner - Auto
Georgia SB 121 (2025, as passed/signed) - DUI minimums

states.note: Georgia requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries you cause, plus $25,000 for property damage. Georgia is an at-fault state with no required PIP. We haven't yet confirmed the uninsured-motorist rule from the official code.
states.uncertain: Whether uninsured motorist coverage is included is left blank. The official Georgia code (O.C.G.A. 33-7-11) is published only through LexisNexis, which we couldn't open. Unofficial copies of that section say uninsured-motorist coverage is included unless a named insured rejects it in writing, but we don't cite unofficial copies. That PIP and medical payments coverage are not required is inferred from the insurance department page listing only liability, not from an explicit statement.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage is included at the bodily injury limits in HRS 431:10C-301(b)(1) (now $40,000/$80,000) unless a named insured rejects it in writing. Underinsured motorist coverage must also be included and can be rejected in writing, with a signature next to or below the offer.
states.effective: Limits rose from 20/40/10 to 40/80/20 for new and renewal policies effective on or after January 1, 2026 (L 2024, c 138). PIP stays at $10,000.

sources.label: Hawaii Insurance Division - FAQ: Auto Insurance Minimum Limits (Effective January 1, 2026)

states.note: Since January 1, 2026, Hawaii requires at least $40,000 per person and $80,000 per accident for injuries, plus $20,000 for property damage (up from 20/40/10). You also need $10,000 of personal injury protection, which pays your own medical bills no matter who caused the crash. Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage are included unless you turn them down in writing.
states.uncertain: The HRS pages are from the 'hrscurrent' site, which was read through a browser because direct downloads hit a Cloudflare block. The session-law citation (L 2024, c 138) comes from the section's history note; the Act itself was not opened to confirm its effective-date clause, but the Insurance Division FAQ confirms January 1, 2026.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage must be included at least at the 49-117 bodily injury limits (25/50). A named insured can reject either or both in writing or electronically.
states.effective: 25/50/15 is unchanged. Idaho Code 49-117 was last amended in 2022 (ch. 98), and 41-2502 in 2009. No 2025-2026 bill changing the limits was found. The Dept. of Insurance issued Bulletin 26-07 on July 1, 2026 about household exclusions and step-down provisions; it does not change the minimums.

sources.label: Idaho Code 49-117 (definition of proof of financial responsibility)

states.note: Idaho requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $15,000 for property damage. Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage are included unless you turn them down in writing. Idaho is an at-fault state with no required PIP.
states.uncertain: No 2025 or 2026 bill changing the Idaho minimums was found, but the 2026 bill list was not searched exhaustively. That PIP and medical payments coverage are not required is inferred because no Idaho statute requires them.

states.umLimits: Every liability policy must include uninsured motorist coverage at least at the 7-203 limits (25/50), and that minimum uninsured motorist coverage cannot be rejected. By default uninsured motorist coverage matches your bodily injury limits; you can reject only the amount above 25/50, in writing. Underinsured motorist coverage is required only when your uninsured motorist coverage is above the 7-203 minimum, and then it must equal your uninsured motorist coverage amount. A minimum 25/50/20 policy therefore needs no underinsured motorist coverage.
states.effective: 25/50/20 applies to policies issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2015. The latest amendment to 7-203 (P.A. 102-982, eff. 7-1-23) only changed wording ('crash'). No change is scheduled.

sources.label: 625 ILCS 5/7-203 (requirements as to policy or bond)

states.note: Illinois requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $20,000 for property damage. Uninsured-motorist coverage at 25/50 is always included and can't be turned down. If you buy higher limits, underinsured-motorist coverage is added to match.
states.uncertain: Underinsured motorist coverage is marked not required for a minimum 25/50/20 policy only. Under 143a-2, underinsured motorist coverage becomes required whenever uninsured motorist coverage is above 25/50, and uninsured motorist coverage defaults to your bodily injury limits unless you reject the excess in writing.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage must be included at limits at least equal to your bodily injury limits unless rejected in writing, together or separately. Underinsured motorist coverage can't be sold below $50,000. Uninsured motorist property-damage coverage is optional under IC 27-7-5-3, which was not re-read here.
states.effective: Property damage rose from $10,000 to $25,000 on July 1, 2018 (IC 9-25-4-5, as amended by P.L.24-2017). No 2024-2026 change appears in the 2026 Indiana Code.

sources.label: IC 9-25-4-5 (minimum amounts of financial responsibility), 2026 Indiana Code
Indiana BMV - Proof of Financial Responsibility
IC 27-7-5-2 (UM/UIM required coverage; rejection), 2026 Indiana Code
Indiana Department of Insurance - Auto Insurance

states.note: Indiana requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage are included unless you turn them down in writing. Underinsured coverage is at least $50,000.
states.uncertain: The Indiana Code text was read by loading iga.in.gov/ic/2026/Title_9.html and Title_27.html in a browser (the site needs JavaScript). That PIP and medical payments coverage are not required is inferred because no Indiana statute requires them.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage (including hit-and-run) and underinsured motorist coverage must each be included at least at the 321A.1(11) bodily injury limits (20/40). The named insured can reject all of it, or uninsured motorist coverage or underinsured motorist coverage alone, with a signed written rejection on a separate sheet.
states.effective: 20/40/15 applies as printed in Iowa Code 2026. Bills in the 91st General Assembly would raise it to 50/100/25 (SF 119, HF 6, SF 2073, HF 129 renumbered as HF 2352). HF 2352 was 'placed on calendar' on Feb. 9, 2026 with no later action shown. None enacted as of the bill-history pages checked.

sources.label: Iowa Code 516A.1 (UM/UIM in every liability policy; rejection)
Iowa Legislature - bill history SF 119 / HF 6 / HF 129 / HF 2352 (91st GA)

states.note: Iowa requires at least $20,000 per person and $40,000 per accident for injuries, plus $15,000 for property damage. These are among the lowest in the country. Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage are included unless you turn them down in writing.
states.uncertain: Bills to raise the minimums to 50/100/25 were pending in 2026. The bill history shows no passage, but a late-session law effective July 1, 2026 could have been missed; checking Iowa Acts 2026 would confirm. PIP and medical payments coverage are not required under any Iowa statute found.

states.pipAmount: Minimums: $4,500 medical; $900/month disability/work loss for 1 year; $4,500 rehabilitation; $2,000 funeral; $25/day substitution (in-home services) for 365 days; $900/month survivor benefits
states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage must equal your bodily injury limits, and underinsured motorist coverage is built into uninsured motorist coverage. You can reject in writing only the uninsured motorist coverage amount above the 40-3107 bodily injury minimum (25/50), so the minimum uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage always stays.
states.effective: 25/50/25 applies to policies issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2017 (L. 2016, ch. 72). Starting with the 2026 legislative interim, and at least every 10 years after, a legislative study committee will review whether to change the minimums (40-3107(j)). No change enacted.
states.note: Kansas requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. You also need personal injury protection, which covers at least $4,500 of your own medical bills no matter who caused the crash. Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage at the minimum limits is always included.
states.uncertain: The PIP disability minimum is described as income-related in 40-3103; the $900/month figure is the statutory floor. Whether the 2026 interim study committee met and made recommendations was not checked.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage must be included at least at the 304.39-110 bodily injury limits unless a named insured rejects it in writing. Insurers must only make underinsured motorist coverage available on request, so it is optional.
states.effective: Split limits of 25/50/25, or a $60,000 combined single limit (KRS 304.39-110, eff. June 29, 2017). The $10,000 basic reparation benefit stayed the same when 2026 Ky. Acts ch. 149 (HB 627, eff. July 15, 2026) amended 304.39-020; that Act changed PIP medical-fee and fraud provisions. Underinsured motorist coverage statute 304.39-320 was amended in 2024 (ch. 27, eff. April 2, 2024).

sources.label: KRS 304.39-060 (acceptance or rejection of tort limitation - 'choice no-fault')

states.note: Kentucky requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage, or a $60,000 combined limit. You also need $10,000 of personal injury protection. Kentucky is a 'choice' no-fault state: you're under no-fault rules unless you file a form with the Department of Insurance keeping your full right to sue (and be sued). Uninsured-motorist coverage is included unless you reject it in writing; underinsured coverage is optional.
states.uncertain: Kentucky is a "choice" no-fault state. No-fault is the default: KRS 304.39-060 puts you under it unless you file a written rejection with the Department of Insurance. The tort threshold is more than $1,000 in medical expense or a listed serious injury.

states.umLimits: Uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage is one combined coverage (uninsured or underinsured). By default it equals your bodily-injury liability limits. You can reject it, pick lower limits, or pick economic-only coverage, but only on the commissioner's form signed by the named insured. Limits can't go below the R.S. 32:900 minimums unless you choose economic-only coverage.
states.effective: The 15/30/25 limits in R.S. 32:900 have been in place since Jan. 1, 2010 (Acts 2008, No. 921); the section was last amended in 2011. Act 381 of 2024 (HB 511) changed how insurers verify and keep the uninsured motorist coverage rejection form. HB 434 of 2025 changed R.S. 32:866 ('no pay, no play'): uninsured owners can't recover the first $100,000 of bodily-injury damages or the first $100,000 of property damages (it had been $15,000 and $25,000). The minimum limits didn't change.
states.note: Louisiana requires at least $15,000 per person and $30,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage matches your liability limits unless you reject it or lower it on a signed state form. If you drive without insurance, you can't recover the first $100,000 of your own injury or property damages after a crash.
states.uncertain: HB 434 (2025): we read the enrolled bill, not the codified R.S. 32:866 text, and we did not confirm its effective date. We found no 2026 change to R.S. 32:900 on the legislature site (its history ends with Acts 2011, No. 17). Medical payments coverage is marked not required because no statute we found requires it.

states.umLimits: 'Uninsured vehicle coverage' covers both uninsured and underinsured drivers and can't be dropped. On standard private-passenger policies it must equal your bodily-injury liability limits unless you sign the statutory form choosing lower limits. It can never be below $50,000/$100,000.
states.effective: The current figures appear in 29-A M.R.S. §1605 as shown on the Revisor's site (data extracted Oct. 2025). We found no 2024-2026 change.
states.note: Maine requires at least $50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Every policy must also include at least $2,000 of medical payments coverage and uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage. That coverage matches your liability limits unless you sign a form choosing less.
states.uncertain: The medical-payments requirement in §1605-A doesn't apply to policies that insure more than 4 vehicles or to garage-type policies. The $500 towing coverage in §1605(1)(C) isn't included in this record.

states.pipAmount: At least $2,500 for medical, hospital, and disability benefits, unless the first named insured signs an affirmative written waiver on the commissioner's form.
states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage can't be dropped. Maryland defines an 'uninsured motor vehicle' to include one whose liability limits are below your uninsured motorist coverage limits, so underinsured coverage comes with it. The minimum is the Title 17 liability minimum ($30,000/$60,000 bodily injury and $15,000 property damage). On private-passenger policies uninsured motorist coverage must equal your liability limits unless you sign a written waiver (§19-510). The waiver only lets you go down toward the minimum, not remove the coverage. Enhanced underinsured motorist coverage is available as an option under §19-509.1.
states.effective: 30/60/15 is current under Transp. §17-103. The legislature site shows new versions of Ins. §§19-509 and 19-510 taking effect June 30, 2029 (Ch. 514 of 2023). They cover electing enhanced underinsured coverage in place of standard uninsured motorist coverage. The minimum amounts don't change.
states.note: Maryland requires at least $30,000 per person and $60,000 per accident for injuries, plus $15,000 for property damage. Your policy also includes $2,500 of personal injury protection unless you waive it in writing. Uninsured motorist coverage, which also covers underinsured drivers, can't be dropped.
states.uncertain: It isn't marked as a no-fault state because Maryland PIP pays regardless of fault but no statute we found limits lawsuits (it is add-on PIP). We didn't retrieve a statute on that point. Medical payments coverage is marked not required because no statute we found requires it.

states.pipAmount: $8,000 per person (the §34A definition says 'at least eight thousand dollars').
states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage for bodily injury is compulsory (c.175 §113L(1)) in 'amounts or limits prescribed for bodily injury or death for a liability policy'. We read that as 25/50 for policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2025. Underinsured coverage is optional: the policyholder 'elects to purchase' it and must be told it's available.
states.effective: St. 2024, c. 275 raised the minimums from 20/40 bodily injury and $5,000 property damage to $25,000/$50,000 bodily injury and $30,000 property damage. The increase applies to policies issued or renewed on or after July 1, 2025. PIP stays at $8,000.

sources.label: Mass. G.L. c.90 §34A ('Motor vehicle liability policy' definition)

states.note: For policies issued or renewed since July 1, 2025, Massachusetts requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $30,000 for property damage. Every policy also includes $8,000 of personal injury protection and uninsured motorist coverage. Massachusetts is a no-fault state, so your own PIP pays first after a crash.
states.uncertain: The uninsured motorist coverage minimum of $25,000/$50,000 comes from reading §113L's cross-reference together with the 2024 amendment. Mass.gov returned HTTP 403 to our tools, so we couldn't quote the insurance division's bulletin; a search snippet of mass.gov listed uninsured motorist coverage at $25,000/$50,000. Medical payments coverage is optional as far as we found; it isn't among the compulsory coverages.

states.pipAmount: PIP medical has been a choice since July 2, 2020 (MCL 500.3107c): unlimited, $500,000, $250,000, or $50,000 (only if you're on Medicaid and your household is covered). If you make no valid choice, you get unlimited. Some people with Medicare Parts A and B can opt out of PIP medical entirely (MCL 500.3107d). Property protection insurance (PPI) pays up to $1,000,000 per accident for damage your car does in Michigan (MCL 500.3121).
states.effective: Since July 2, 2020 (2019 no-fault reform), the default bodily injury limits in a Michigan policy are $250,000/$500,000 (MCL 500.3009(1)). You can sign the state's form to choose lower limits, but not below $50,000/$100,000 (MCL 500.3009(5)). Those are the lowest limits you can actually buy. The old 20/40/10 still appears in MCL 257.520 (financial-responsibility certificates) and was the policy minimum before July 2, 2020. The $10,000 property damage figure in 500.3009(1)(c) is unchanged; inside Michigan, PPI covers property damage.

sources.label: Michigan DIFS, 'Michigan's Auto Insurance Law Has Changed' guide (pre-reform edition)

states.note: Michigan policies now start at $250,000 per person and $500,000 per accident for injuries. You can sign a state form to drop that to $50,000/$100,000, the lowest allowed. Every policy includes no-fault personal injury protection (you pick a medical limit) and up to $1 million for damage your car does to property in Michigan. Uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage is optional.
states.uncertain: The injury limits record the lowest limits you can buy (50/100), not the 250/500 default. The $10,000 property-damage figure is the statutory property damage liability limit, which in practice applies outside Michigan; in-state property damage is paid by up to $1 million of property protection insurance (PPI). The DIFS guide confirming uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage is optional is an older pre-2020 edition that still lists 20/40/10; we relied on it only for the uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage point. Medical payments coverage is marked not required because no statute we found requires it.

states.pipAmount: $40,000 per person: $20,000 for medical expenses and $20,000 for income loss, replacement services, funeral, and survivor losses (Minn. Stat. 65B.44).
states.umLimits: Separate uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverages are both required, each at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident (65B.49 subd. 3a). The statute doesn't allow either to be rejected.
states.effective: The current figures appear in the 2025 Minnesota Statutes. HF 2494 / SF 2639 (2025-2026) would have raised them to 60/120 bodily injury and 50/100 uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage. HF 2494 never left committee (last action May 5, 2025), and no enacted change appears on the revisor's page.
states.note: Minnesota requires at least $30,000 per person and $60,000 per accident for injuries, plus $10,000 for property damage. Every policy also includes $40,000 of no-fault personal injury protection ($20,000 medical and $20,000 for lost income and similar losses). Separate uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage is required at $25,000/$50,000 each.
states.uncertain: The 65B.51 quote shows only the $4,000 medical-expense part of the tort threshold (other routes include death, permanent injury, and 60+ days of disability). Medical payments coverage is marked not required because no statute we found requires it; PIP covers medical costs.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist bodily-injury coverage and uninsured motorist property-damage coverage must be included, at no less than the Safety Responsibility Law minimums (25/50 bodily injury, $25,000 property damage), unless a named insured rejects the coverage in writing (Miss. Code 83-11-101). The property damage part may exclude the first $200. The definition of 'uninsured motor vehicle' (83-11-103(c)(iii)) includes an insured vehicle whose bodily injury limits are less than your uninsured motorist coverage limits, so underinsured coverage is part of the same coverage.
states.effective: 25/50/25 has been in effect since Jan. 1, 2006 (per the Mississippi Insurance Department). 2026 HB 382, which would have made uninsured motorist coverage mandatory with no rejection, died in committee on Feb. 3, 2026.

sources.label: Mississippi Insurance Department, Auto Insurance consumer page
Miss. Code 63-15-3(j) (text as reproduced in 2015 HB 303)
Miss. Code 83-11-101 (text as reproduced in 2026 HB 382, died in committee)
Miss. Code 83-11-103(c)(iii) (text as reproduced in 2020 HB 1046)

states.note: Mississippi requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Uninsured motorist coverage, which also covers underinsured drivers, is included unless you turn it down in writing.
states.uncertain: The official Mississippi Code is hosted on LexisNexis, which direct downloads couldn't fetch, so statute text comes from legislature bill documents that reproduce the sections. In HB 382 the rejection sentences are marked for deletion, which shows they are current law; formatting was lost in the text extraction. The 83-11-103 text comes from a 2020 introduced bill and may have been lightly amended since. Medical payments coverage is optional according to the Mississippi Insurance Department's consumer page.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist bodily-injury coverage is required on private-passenger policies at no less than the 303.030 bodily injury limits ($25,000/$50,000). No statute provides a way to reject it; for commercial vehicles and fleets of 5 or more it only has to be offered. Underinsured motorist coverage is optional (379.204 only covers how underinsured motorist coverage is construed if you buy it).
states.effective: RSMo 303.190 has been effective since July 1, 2019, 303.025 since Jan. 1, 2024, and 379.203 since Aug. 28, 1991. We found no change to the minimum amounts in 2024-2026.

sources.label: Missouri Department of Revenue, Insurance Information

states.note: Missouri requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Every personal auto policy must also include uninsured motorist coverage of at least $25,000/$50,000. Underinsured motorist coverage is optional.
states.uncertain: Marking underinsured motorist coverage as not required rests on finding no statute that requires underinsured motorist coverage; 379.204 only regulates underinsured motorist coverage when it is purchased. Medical payments coverage is marked not required because no statute we found requires it.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist bodily-injury coverage must be included at the 61-6-103 limits ($25,000/$50,000) unless the named insured rejects it (MCA 33-23-201). After a rejection, renewals don't need to include it unless you ask in writing.
states.effective: The figures appear in MCA 61-6-103 (Montana Code Annotated 2025). We found no 2024-2026 change.
states.note: Montana requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $20,000 for property damage. Uninsured motorist coverage is included unless you sign a form turning it down. Underinsured motorist coverage is optional.
states.uncertain: MCA 33-23-201 says only that the named insured 'has the right to reject' uninsured motorist coverage; it doesn't say 'in writing'. The signed-form requirement comes from the CSI page, which we read through a summarizing tool because direct downloads were blocked by Cloudflare. Underinsured motorist coverage is marked not required: we found no Montana statute requiring underinsured motorist coverage, but no primary source we retrieved says it is optional. Medical payments coverage is marked not required because no statute we found requires it.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage each at least $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident (bodily injury). Insurer must provide higher limits on written request, up to $100,000/$300,000.
states.effective: No 2024-2026 change found; current text of Neb. Rev. Stat. 60-310 and 44-6408 as published by the Nebraska Legislature.
states.note: Nebraska requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Every policy must also include uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage of at least $25,000/$50,000; there is no written opt-out in the statute.
states.uncertain: Absence of a PIP or medical payments coverage requirement is inferred from the statutes reviewed (no requirement found); not stated affirmatively by a primary source.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage must be at least the chapter 485 bodily-injury minimums ($25,000/$50,000). Insurers must offer uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage equal to the policy's bodily-injury limits (NRS 687B.145(2)); underinsured motorist coverage is offered, not mandated.
states.effective: NRS 485.185 last amended 2017; NRS chapter 485 page is revised through the 2025 session (Rev. 4/15/2026) and shows no change to the 25/50/20 limits.
states.note: Nevada requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $20,000 for property damage. Uninsured-motorist coverage is included unless you turn it down in writing; underinsured-motorist and medical-payments coverage must be offered but are optional.
states.uncertain: Classifying underinsured motorist coverage as optional rests on NRS 687B.145(2) ('must offer'); NRS 690B.020 mandates only uninsured/hit-and-run coverage. Nevada's statutory uninsured motorist coverage definition in 690B.020(3)(b) treats vehicles with liability below the NRS 485.210 minimum as uninsured, which is not the same as underinsured motorist coverage.

states.umLimits: If you buy a policy, uninsured motorist coverage must be at least the liability minimums ($25,000/$50,000) and automatically equals your liability limits if you buy higher. NH's uninsured motorist coverage definition (RSA 259:117) includes underinsured vehicles, so underinsured motorist coverage is part of the same required coverage.
states.effective: RSA 259:61 last amended 2016; RSA 264:20 unchanged since 1982. No 2024-2026 change found.

sources.label: NH Insurance Department, 2022 Automobile Insurance Consumer Guide
RSA 264:20 (amount of proof of financial responsibility)

states.note: New Hampshire doesn't require most drivers to buy car insurance, but you're still on the hook for crash damages, and the state can require insurance after a crash or violation. If you do buy a policy, it must include at least $25,000/$50,000 for injuries, $25,000 for property damage, $1,000 of medical payments, and uninsured-motorist coverage (which also covers underinsured drivers).
states.uncertain: The “required” marks for uninsured, underinsured, and medical payments coverage apply only when you buy a policy, since insurance itself is optional for most drivers. The NH Insurance Department guide is dated 2022; the statutes it relies on were confirmed current on gc.nh.gov.

states.pipAmount: Standard Policy: at least $15,000 per person/accident (up to $250,000 or more available); up to $250,000 for certain serious injuries regardless of the limit you choose. Basic Policy: $15,000 per person/accident.
states.umLimits: Standard Policy must include uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage at the statutory bodily-injury minimums ($35,000/$70,000 from 2026-01-01) plus uninsured motorist property-damage coverage ($25,000 aggregate, $500 deductible). Higher limits up to your liability limits are optional. Basic Policy includes no uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage.
states.effective: P.L.2022, c.87 raised Standard minimums: 15/30 before 2023-01-01; 25/50/25 for policies issued or renewed 2023-01-01 to 2025-12-31; 35/70/25 for policies issued or renewed on or after 2026-01-01. Figures above are the current 2026 Standard Policy minimums.

sources.label: N.J.S.A. 17:28-1.1 as amended by P.L.2022, c.87
NJ DOBI, Auto Insurance New Jersey Buyer's Guide (2026)

states.note: With a Standard Policy, New Jersey requires at least $35,000 per person and $70,000 per accident for injuries, $25,000 for property damage, at least $15,000 of PIP, and uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage. A cheaper Basic Policy is also legal: it carries $15,000 PIP and $5,000 property damage, with injury liability only as an optional $10,000, and it gives you much less protection.
states.uncertain: New Jersey is a "choice" state: with a Standard Policy you pick the limited or unlimited right to sue (the Basic Policy always has the limited right). We haven't confirmed from an official copy of N.J.S.A. 39:6A-8.1 which option applies if you don't choose, so the default is left blank. The PIP $15,000 minimum and Basic Policy figures ($5,000 property damage, optional $10,000 injury liability) come from the DOBI 2026 Buyer's Guide; the underlying statutes (N.J.S.A. 39:6A-4, 39:6A-3.1) were not read directly.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage, which by statute includes underinsured motorist coverage, must be at least the 66-5-215 minimums (25/50 bodily injury and $10,000 property damage, with up to a $250 property damage exclusion). Higher limits up to your liability limits are available. The named insured may reject it, and the rejection must be in writing and made part of the policy (13.12.3.9 NMAC).
states.effective: No change found. 2025 bills to raise minimums (SB 319) and to remove the uninsured motorist coverage rejection right (HB 97) both died in the 2025 regular session.

sources.label: NM MVD FAQ: What automobile insurance am I required to have
NMSA 66-5-301 (current text as reproduced in 2025 HB 97 committee substitute, which died)

states.note: New Mexico requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $10,000 for property damage. Uninsured-motorist coverage, which also covers underinsured drivers, is included unless you turn it down in writing.
states.uncertain: We couldn't load the official NMSA compilation (NMOneSource) directly. The limits come from NM MVD pages that quote 66-5-208, and the 66-5-301 wording comes from the existing-law text shown in the 2025 HB 97 substitute; the bracketed rejection clause there was existing law that the bill, which died, would have deleted. The 66-5-215 figures were not read from the statute itself.

states.pipAmount: $50,000 per person basic economic loss (mandatory no-fault)
states.umLimits: Mandatory uninsured motorist coverage: $25,000 injury / $50,000 death per person; $50,000 injury / $100,000 death per accident. Supplementary uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage (SUM) is optional at the insured's option, up to bodily injury limits (max $250,000/$500,000).
states.effective: No 2024-2026 change found in VTL 311 as published by the NY Senate. Death limits are higher: $50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident.

sources.label: NY Department of Financial Services, "How much auto insurance must I carry?" (plain-language fallback)

states.note: New York requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries ($50,000/$100,000 if someone dies), plus $10,000 for property damage. Your policy also must include $50,000 of no-fault (PIP) coverage and basic uninsured-motorist coverage; underinsured-motorist (SUM) coverage is optional.
states.uncertain: The duty to carry no-fault (Ins. Law 5103) was not read directly; the $50,000 figure is from Ins. Law 5102(a).

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist bodily-injury coverage defaults to your highest bodily injury liability limit (up to $1M). You may choose lower limits but not below the $50,000/$100,000 minimums. Uninsured motorist property-damage coverage defaults to your property damage limit. Underinsured motorist coverage must equal your uninsured motorist coverage bodily-injury limits.
states.effective: Raised from 30/60/25 to 50/100/50 by S.L. 2023-133 s.12. S.L. 2024-29 s.8(c) changed the effective date from Jan 1, 2025 to July 1, 2025, for policies issued or renewed on or after that date. The same law made uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage mandatory.
states.note: Since July 1, 2025, North Carolina requires at least $50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident for injuries, plus $50,000 for property damage. Every policy must also include uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage, which by default match your liability limits.
states.uncertain: The session-law HTML shows the struck-through 'January 1, 2025' and the inserted 'July 1, 2025' as plain text. Reading 'July 1, 2025' as the operative date follows NC strike/insert convention. Absence of a medical payments coverage requirement is inferred (none found).

states.pipAmount: $30,000 per person basic no-fault benefits (max $150/week work loss; $3,500 funeral)
states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage at least the 39-16.1-11 limits ($25,000/$50,000); underinsured motorist coverage must equal uninsured motorist coverage limits. Higher limits on request, up to bodily injury limits or $100,000/$300,000.
states.effective: No 2024-2026 change found in the current NDCC chapter PDFs.
states.note: North Dakota requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. It is a no-fault state: your policy must include $30,000 of no-fault (PIP) benefits, plus uninsured and underinsured motorist coverage.

states.effective: ORC 4509.01 effective April 15, 2021 (no limit change); 4509.101 effective Sept 30, 2025 (HB 96, penalties/administration, not limits). No 2024-2026 change to 25/50/25 found.
states.note: Ohio requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Uninsured- and underinsured-motorist coverage is optional, so ask for it if you want it.
states.uncertain: Proof of financial responsibility can also be a bond, deposit, or self-insurance, not only an insurance policy. Absence of a medical payments coverage requirement is inferred (none found).

states.umLimits: At least the bodily-injury minimums (25/50) unless rejected in writing; higher limits up to your liability limits must be offered. Oklahoma's 'uninsured motor vehicle' definition includes underinsured vehicles, so uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage are one combined coverage.
states.effective: 25/50/25 minimums in 47 O.S. 7-324; uninsured motorist coverage statute references April 1, 2005 as the date the 25/50 uninsured motorist coverage minimum applied. No 2024-2026 change found on OSCN.
states.note: Oklahoma requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Uninsured-motorist coverage, which also covers drivers who don't carry enough insurance, comes with your policy unless you turn it down in writing.
states.uncertain: Marking PIP and medical payments coverage not required is based on no statutory PIP/medical payments coverage mandate appearing in the compulsory-insurance and uninsured motorist coverage statutes reviewed; no separate primary source affirmatively saying 'not required' was located.

states.pipAmount: Personal injury protection on private passenger vehicle policies: medical/hospital and related expenses up to $15,000 per person (ORS 742.524), plus other PIP benefits listed in that section.
states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage must equal your bodily-injury liability limits unless you elect lower limits in writing, never below the 25/50 minimums in ORS 806.070. Underinsured motorist coverage is part of the required uninsured motorist coverage. Statute does not allow rejecting uninsured motorist coverage entirely.
states.effective: ORS 2025 edition. Property damage $20,000 (amounts last amended 2009 c.66 per history note). No 2024-2026 change found.
states.note: Oregon requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $20,000 for property damage. Every car policy also has to include personal injury protection (at least $15,000 for medical bills) and uninsured/underinsured-motorist coverage.
states.uncertain: It isn't marked as a no-fault state because no tort-threshold provision was found alongside the PIP statutes (Oregon PIP is add-on); not confirmed by an explicit primary statement. Medical payments coverage isn't separately addressed; PIP covers medical expenses.

states.umLimits: Insurers must offer uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage, but buying them is optional (75 Pa.C.S. 1731). Lower limits can be requested under section 1734.
states.effective: 15/30/5 financial responsibility definition in 75 Pa.C.S. 1702; no 2024-2026 change found.
states.note: Pennsylvania requires at least $15,000 per person and $30,000 per accident for injuries, plus $5,000 for property damage, and every policy includes a $5,000 medical benefit. Uninsured and underinsured-motorist coverage must be offered to you but is optional. You also choose between 'full tort' and 'limited tort', which affects your right to sue for pain and suffering.
states.uncertain: Pennsylvania is a "choice" state: you pick full tort or limited tort (75 Pa.C.S. 1705). If you don't choose, the law presumes full tort, so the default is not no-fault. The required $5,000 first-party medical benefit is recorded as PIP; there is no separate medical payments coverage mandate.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage must equal your bodily-injury limits. You can pick lower limits in writing, but not below 25/50. You can drop it to zero only if you buy just the state minimum liability coverage and sign an advisory notice. Uninsured motorist coverage includes underinsured motorists. The property-damage part of uninsured motorist coverage can be rejected in writing.
states.effective: 31-47-2 amounts last amended by P.L. 2014 per history note; no 2024-2026 change found.
states.note: Rhode Island requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage (or a $75,000 combined limit). Uninsured/underinsured-motorist coverage comes with your policy. You can drop it only if you buy just the state minimum and sign a written warning notice.
states.uncertain: The uninsured motorist mark is a best fit: written opt-out is available only to buyers of minimum-limit policies. PIP/medical payments coverage 'not required' is based on no mandate appearing in the chapters reviewed.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage is mandatory at no less than 25/50 bodily injury and $25,000 property damage (the first $200 of property loss may be excluded). Insurers must offer higher uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage up to your liability limits, but underinsured motorist coverage is optional.
states.effective: 25/50/25 since 2006 Act No. 395, for policies issued or renewed on or after Jan 1, 2007. Uninsured motorist coverage minimums raised by 2013 Act No. 47, effective Jan 1, 2014. The option to pay a fee and register an uninsured vehicle (56-10-510) was removed by 2023 Act No. 51, effective July 1, 2024.
states.note: South Carolina requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Uninsured-motorist coverage is mandatory. Underinsured-motorist coverage must be offered to you but is optional.
states.uncertain: Marking PIP not required is based on no PIP mandate appearing in Title 38 Ch. 77. Medical payments coverage is optional: a Ch. 77 provision refers to medical payments coverage offered 'at the option of the insured'.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage must each equal your bodily-injury liability limits, but the required amount is capped at 100/300 unless you ask for more. There is no written-rejection option in the statutes. So at the 25/50 minimum you carry 25/50 uninsured motorist coverage and 25/50 underinsured motorist coverage.
states.effective: Statute source notes show no amendments to 32-35-70 since 1992 or to 58-11-9.4 since 1997; no 2024-2026 change found.
states.note: South Dakota requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Every policy must also include uninsured and underinsured-motorist coverage at the same limits as your injury liability.
states.uncertain: Text was read through the legislature's API endpoint (sdlegislature.gov/api/Statutes/<section>.html); the listed URLs are the public pages for the same sections. PIP/medical payments coverage 'not required' is based on no mandate appearing in the sections reviewed.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage must equal your bodily-injury limits unless you reject it completely in writing, or pick lower limits in writing (not below the 55-12-107 minimums).
states.effective: Property damage rose from $15,000 to $25,000 and the single-limit option rose to $65,000 for proof required after Dec 31, 2022 (2022 Pub. Ch. 860). Existing policies had until their first renewal after that date.

sources.label: Tennessee Department of Revenue - Financial Responsibility Law
T.C.A. 56-7-1201 (Lexis public access, search for the section)

states.note: Tennessee requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage (or a $65,000 combined limit). Uninsured-motorist coverage is included at your liability limits unless you turn it down in writing.
states.uncertain: The official T.C.A. Site (Lexis) blocked full-document access with a captcha. Only the search-result excerpt of 56-7-1201(a)(3) was read verbatim, plus the fragment '(a)(1) Every automobile liab...'. Not confirmed from a primary source: whether TN's uninsured motorist coverage definition (56-7-1202) covers underinsured vehicles (so underinsured motorist coverage is left blank), and the exact wording of 55-12-139 (compulsory insurance). That insurance is required rests on the Dept. of Revenue page. PIP/medical payments coverage 'not required' is based on no mandate being found.

states.pipAmount: Statute does not require insurers to provide more than $2,500 per person in aggregate PIP benefits (Ins. Code 1952.153); $2,500 is the standard amount.
states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage are one combined coverage in Texas (Ins. Code 1952.101), at least the Chapter 601 limits (30/60/25), including property damage.
states.effective: 30/60/25 effective January 1, 2011 (Transp. Code 601.072(a-1)); no change found for 2024-2026.

sources.label: Texas Department of Insurance, Auto insurance guide

states.note: Texas requires at least $30,000 per person and $60,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Personal injury protection (PIP) and uninsured/underinsured-motorist coverage come with your policy unless you turn them down in writing.
states.uncertain: Texas is an at-fault (tort) state even though PIP is included by default; not marking it no-fault is based on the statute's structure (no tort threshold), not an explicit statement. Medical payments coverage is not addressed as a requirement in the statutes reviewed; recorded as not required.

states.pipAmount: At least $3,000 per person for medical expenses, plus other listed benefits (e.g., $3,000 death benefit) (Utah Code 31A-22-307).
states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage default to your liability limits (or the insurer's maximum, if lower). You can reject them or buy lower limits by signing an acknowledgment form. Uninsured motorist coverage may not be sold below the 31A-22-304 bodily-injury minimums.
states.effective: Policies issued or renewed on or after Jan 1, 2025: 30/65/25 or a $90,000 combined single limit. Through Dec 31, 2024 it was 25/65/15 or $80,000. 31A-22-302, -305, -305.3 and -309 were amended in the 2026 General Session (effective 5/6/2026); the 304 limits were not changed.
states.note: Utah requires at least $30,000 per person and $65,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage, on policies issued or renewed since January 1, 2025. Your policy also must include $3,000 of personal injury protection. Uninsured and underinsured-motorist coverage are included unless you turn them down in writing.
states.uncertain: The compulsory-owner's-security statute (41-12a-301) was not fetched directly; that insurance is required relies on 31A-22-302 referring to 'the owner's or operator's security requirement of Section 41-12a-301'. Medical payments coverage has no separate mandate (PIP covers medical).

states.umLimits: Uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage is mandatory, at least $50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident for bodily injury, plus up to $10,000 for property damage ($150 deductible). If your liability limits are higher, uninsured motorist coverage matches them unless you direct otherwise. Uninsured motorist coverage and underinsured motorist coverage are one combined coverage (23 V.S.A. 941).
states.effective: Vermont Statutes Online reflects the 2025 session; history shows the last amendment to 800 effective July 1, 2024 (not to the dollar amounts). No 2026 change to the limits was found, but the online code may not yet include 2026 acts.
states.note: Vermont requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $10,000 for property damage. Every policy must also include uninsured/underinsured-motorist coverage of at least $50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident.
states.uncertain: The Vermont Statutes Online disclaimer says it includes actions through the 2025 session; 2026 session acts were not checked against the codified text. PIP/medical payments coverage 'not required' is based on no mandate appearing in Chapter 11.

states.umLimits: Uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage is one endorsement (Va. Code 38.2-2206). Limits must be at least the 46.2-472 minimums (50/100/25) and equal your liability limits unless you reject the additional coverage above the minimum. Underinsured motorist coverage limits equal uninsured motorist coverage limits.
states.effective: 50/100/25 for policies effective on or after January 1, 2025 (was 30/60/20 for policies effective 2022-01-01 through 2024-12-31). The option to pay an uninsured motor vehicle fee instead of buying insurance ended July 1, 2024.

sources.label: Virginia DMV, New Laws Take Effect July 1, 2024

states.note: For policies starting on or after January 1, 2025, Virginia requires at least $50,000 per person and $100,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Uninsured/underinsured-motorist coverage at those minimums is always included. Since July 1, 2024, you can no longer pay a fee to drive uninsured.
states.uncertain: The date the uninsured motor vehicle fee ended comes from the Virginia DMV announcement; the repealing act (2023 session, SB 951 per DMV/LIS search results) was not read directly. Only uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage above the statutory minimum can be rejected; the minimum uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage itself has no opt-out in 38.2-2206(A).

states.pipAmount: Insurers must offer PIP with at least $10,000 medical/hospital, $2,000 funeral, $10,000 income continuation (max $200/week), and $5,000 loss of services (max $200/week) (RCW 48.22.095). You can reject it in writing.
states.umLimits: Washington's 'underinsured motor vehicle' definition includes vehicles with no insurance, so one coverage handles both (RCW 48.22.030). Bodily-injury limits equal your liability limits unless you reject all or part in writing.
states.effective: 25/50/10 unchanged since 1980 (RCW 46.29.090 history); no 2024-2026 change found. RCW 46.30.020 was amended by 2025 c 332 but the minimum amounts still reference RCW 46.29.090.
states.note: Washington requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $10,000 for property damage. Underinsured-motorist coverage (which also covers uninsured drivers) is included unless you reject it in writing. Your insurer must offer PIP, and you have to reject it in writing if you don't want it.
states.uncertain: PIP: RCW 48.22.085 calls PIP an 'optional coverage' that must be offered, but rejecting it takes a written rejection, so in practice it works much like 'included unless rejected in writing.' We record it as not required because the statute's word is 'optional.'

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage at least the 17D-4-2 minimums (25/50/25); may exclude the first $300 of property damage. Insurers must offer optional higher uninsured motorist coverage up to 100/300/50 and optional underinsured coverage (W. Va. Code 33-6-31(b)).
states.effective: 25/50/25 beginning January 1, 2016 (was 20/40/10). No 2024-2026 change found.
states.note: West Virginia requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $25,000 for property damage. Uninsured-motorist coverage at those amounts is always part of your policy; underinsured-motorist coverage is an option your insurer has to offer.
states.uncertain: Marking underinsured motorist coverage as not required rests on 33-6-31(b) wording that the policy 'shall provide an option' for underinsured coverage. The statute has no general PIP or medical payments coverage requirement. No-fault status is inferred from the absence of any PIP or tort-threshold statute.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist coverage at least $25,000 per person / $50,000 per accident (bodily injury) (s. 632.32(4)(a)1). Underinsured motorist coverage is optional: insurers must give notice that it's available, and if you accept it the limits must be at least $50,000 / $100,000 (s. 632.32(4m)). Medical payments coverage at least $1,000 per person unless rejected.
states.effective: 25/50/10 in s. 344.33(2) and s. 344.01(2)(d); no 2024-2026 change found. Current uninsured, underinsured, and medical payments rules reflect 2011 Wisconsin Act 14 (underinsured motorist coverage notice applies to policies effective after Nov. 1, 2011).
states.note: Wisconsin requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $10,000 for property damage. Uninsured-motorist coverage is always included, and $1,000 of medical payments coverage is included unless you turn it down. Underinsured-motorist coverage is optional.
states.uncertain: Medical payments coverage: s. 632.32(4)(bc) says the named insured 'may reject' medical payments coverage but does not say the first rejection must be in writing (only that a later request to restore it on renewal must be written). So it's recorded as “included unless you decline,” not “in writing.” One exception: town mutual policies are exempt from the uninsured motorist coverage requirement.

states.umLimits: Uninsured motorist bodily-injury coverage at least 25/50 (limits of W.S. 31-9-102(a)(xi)). No property-damage uninsured motorist coverage requirement.
states.effective: 25/50/20 per W.S. 31-9-405(b) and 31-9-102(a)(xi) in the official Title 31 compilation (PDF dated May 8, 2026); no 2024-2026 change found.
states.note: Wyoming requires at least $25,000 per person and $50,000 per accident for injuries, plus $20,000 for property damage. Uninsured-motorist coverage comes with your policy unless you turn it down.
states.uncertain: Uninsured motorist coverage: W.S. 31-10-101 says 'The named insured may reject the coverage' without requiring the first rejection to be in writing (only a later request to restore it on renewal must be written). So it's recorded as “included unless you decline,” not “in writing.” We found no underinsured motorist requirement in Title 31; Title 26 (Insurance Code) was not checked for an offer requirement.
